kernel_of_truth: The dome's 'Van Camp 1999' shorthand points at a real empirical fact: the Membach SG (operated by Michel Van Camp at the Royal Observatory of Belgium) genuinely recorded no eclipse-related gravity change during the 11 August 1999 eclipse, exactly as the peer-reviewed record (Mansinha et al. 2001) reports. The dome got the null itself right, and its instinct to attach the Membach result to Van Camp's name has a real-world basis — he is the instrument's custodian scientist. Our own review, not the dome, invented the fuller dead citation.
why_kernel_doesnt_save_claim: A correct null with a wrong attribution still cuts against the dome: the null is the standard-physics prediction (smooth tidal forces, no shadow effect), and under the dome's own kappa = 1.677 nT/uGal it should NOT have been null (3-9 uGal predicted at contact phases). Fixing the citation chain strengthens, not weakens, WIN-013's 'Refuted by Data' verdict — the refutation now rests on a verified, resolvable source. And the dome's citation defect remains real, just thinner than we claimed: a bare attribution to a paper that does not exist under that author-year.

anticipated_objections.objection: Dome defender: 'Your own review fabricated the dead DOI and blamed us — why should anyone trust the rest of your citations?'
anticipated_objections.response: Accepted and owned: the correction is inline and explicit in both WIN-013 and part6, and the full audit trail (ISS-2638, ISS-2645, EXP-601, EXP-603) is public. The asymmetry stands: when our review errs, the error gets found by our own adversarial pipeline and corrected loudly with provenance; the dome's 'Van Camp 1999' citation has stood uncorrected on its site through every version since publication. The test of a review is not zero errors, it is whether errors survive.

anticipated_objections.objection: Dome defender: 'Removing the 1-Hz un-decimated inspection claim concedes the Chebychev rescue — maybe the filter DID hide the pulse.'
anticipated_objections.response: No: the closure now rests on the two facts that never depended on the phantom paper. The IGETS Level-1 1-Hz Membach archive is public and is not subject to the Level-3 decimation filter — anyone including the dome author can search it, no published reanalysis finds the 3-9 uGal feature, and the dome declines to perform the reanalysis its own rescue invites. And the rescue remains self-defeating: the same filter family would have band-stopped the Mohe 1997 valleys out of kappa’s numerator.

anticipated_objections.objection: Curmudgeon: 'Inline corrections clutter the prose; why not fix silently and log in the changelog?'
anticipated_objections.response: Deliberate: this review attacks the dome for silently rewriting its claims (Part 1.4, Timestamp Error tab). Silently rewriting our own fabricated attribution would hand the dome a tu-quoque. The inline parentheticals are one sentence each; the credibility insurance is worth the words. Decider may additionally changelog them.

proposed_integration_patches.find_exact: What Van Camp actually found. The dome cites 'Van Camp 1999. 0.0 μGal. Confirms electromagnetic, not gravitational.' The actual paper (Van Camp et al., 2001, J. Geodetic Soc. Japan) measured gravity at four SG stations during the August 1999 eclipse and found 'no identifiable eclipse-related change above the ambient noise.' The authors concluded this sets an upper bound on gravitational shielding (γ < 10−16 m² kg−1), consistent with standard physics predictions. Van Camp did not conclude 'electromagnetic, not gravitational' — that interpretation is the dome's addition.
proposed_integration_patches.replace_with: What the published record actually shows. The dome cites 'Van Camp 1999. 0.0 μGal. Confirms electromagnetic, not gravitational.' No Van Camp-authored eclipse-gravimetry paper exists under that citation; the peer-reviewed record of the Membach null is Mansinha, Ducarme, Hinderer, Meurers & van Ruymbeke (2001), J. Geod. Soc. Japan 47(1), 387–391. (Michel Van Camp operates the Membach superconducting gravimeter for the Royal Observatory of Belgium — the likely source of the dome's shorthand — but he is not an author.) That paper measured gravity at four SG stations during the August 1999 eclipse and found 'no identifiable eclipse related change above the ambient noise.' The authors concluded this sets an upper bound on gravitational shielding (γ < 10−16 m² kg−1), consistent with standard physics predictions. The paper did not conclude 'electromagnetic, not gravitational' — that interpretation is the dome's addition.

proposed_integration_patches.find_exact: First, the 1999-eclipse SG analysis the dome itself cites is built on raw 1-Hz records, not just Level-3 residuals. Van Camp et al. (2001) — the dedicated minute-timescale Membach reduction that anchors the Mansinha 2001 ensemble and supplies WIN-013’s 0.0 µGal null — explicitly inspects the un-decimated 1-Hz SG output across the C1–C4 interval. A pre-decimation Chebychev low-pass cannot have band-stopped a signal that the published analysis explicitly inspects in the un-decimated record; the rescue applies to a data product (Level-3) that is not the data product the published null was extracted from.
proposed_integration_patches.replace_with: First, the 1999-eclipse SG analysis the dome itself cites was a dedicated eclipse-window search, not a generic archival data product. Mansinha et al. (2001) — the four-station analysis that supplies WIN-013’s 0.0 µGal null — describe their reduction as the residual gravity series “after removal of the theoretical tide and correction for barometric effects,” examined specifically for an eclipse-related change across the eclipse interval; they report none above ambient noise. Nothing in that published reduction confines the search to a decimated Level-3 product, and an analysis purpose-built to hunt for an eclipse signal in the residual series is exactly where a 3–9 µGal pulse — 30–900× the SG noise floor on the dome’s own arithmetic — would have surfaced. (Correction: an earlier revision of this paragraph attributed an un-decimated 1-Hz inspection to a separate “Van Camp et al. (2001)” Membach reduction. No such paper exists and that claim has been withdrawn; the closure of this rescue rests on the published Mansinha reduction plus the two facts following.)
